real_s1.explanation: None of this unit's distinctive-looking effects held up on new photos. In the original table it seemed much less active on noticeably tilted scenes (rows 31, 33). It also seemed to prefer medium over bright lighting (row 22) and subjects fully inside the frame (row 13). On 125 new photos, all four of these picked rows fell below the 95th percentile. The tilt rows rested on only 8 tilted photos, and the lighting effect vanished entirely (d -0.01). The preference for subjects fully inside the frame was steady at the 88th percentile both times, so it is real but not unusual for this layer. The strongest remaining effects are subjects facing toward or away from the camera (rows 2, 4) and level lines over no straight lines (row 32). Similar units share these at the 95th percentile or above, so they describe the group rather than this unit. None of the rows can confidently be said to describe what is particular to this unit.

real_s2.explanation: This unit responds to a group of classes that is mostly dogs (mountain dogs, herding dogs, terriers) along with bovids, buses, swans and similar. Within those classes, no photo property clearly singles it out. On the original photos it seemed suppressed by noticeably tilted horizons or lines, but on new photos that effect fell to the 74th percentile, while the similar units kept it. So the tilt preference is weak here and shared with its neighbours. Its preference for subjects facing toward or away from the camera is also shared by the similar units. Its mild preferences for medium over bright lighting and for subjects fully inside the frame did not reach an unusual level on the new photos. The fully-inside preference stayed consistent but modest, at the 88th percentile both times. None of its within-class preferences is both reliable and particular to this unit.

real_s3.explanation: The unit's clearest, best-supported tendency is one it shares with its most similar units. It is more active when the main subject faces toward or away from the camera than when it faces sideways, especially to the left. It is also more active on photos with level horizons or straight lines than on photos with no visible lines. The apparent penalty for tilted lines rested on only 8 photos and did not replicate on new photos. The preference for medium over bright lighting also did not replicate. No property particular to this unit is reliably established. The weaker hints, a subject fully inside the frame and a subject on the left rather than the right, fall below the threshold for unusual or rest on few photos.
